title: One Percent of Uganda, 65 Percent of Its Tax Revenue: The Extraordinary Story of the Indian Diaspora in Kampala
excerpt: Half a century after Idi Amin expelled 80,000 Asians, Uganda's Indian community generates the majority of the country's income-tax receipts — and the president wants the world to know it
body:
When Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni stood before a packed Diwali celebration in Kampala recently and declared that the Indian community contributes 65 percent of the country's income-tax revenue, he was not merely being generous with a compliment. He was stating an economic fact that has shaped East African policymaking for decades — and one that carries pointed lessons for diaspora communities around the world.

## From Expulsion to Empire

Uganda's Indian story is, at its core, a parable of resilience. In August 1972, the dictator Idi Amin ordered the expulsion of all Asians — roughly 80,000 people, most of Indian origin — giving them 90 days to leave. Businesses were seized. Families that had lived in Uganda for generations were scattered across Britain, Canada, India and elsewhere.

The economic fallout was catastrophic. Factories shuttered. Trade networks collapsed. Uganda's GDP, already fragile, went into freefall. Economists estimate the expulsion set the country back at least a decade.

But the story did not end there. When Museveni took power in 1986 and invited the expelled community to return, a trickle became a flow. Today, an estimated 40,000 people of Indian origin live in Uganda — less than one percent of the population — yet their economic footprint is outsized by any measure.

## The Numbers That Stagger

The 65 percent figure cited by Museveni refers specifically to income-tax receipts, and it reflects the community's dominance in manufacturing, real estate, hospitality and trade. The most prominent example is Dr Sudhir Ruparelia, whose business empire — spanning hotels, insurance, broadcasting and real estate — is valued at roughly $1.6 billion, making him one of East Africa's wealthiest individuals.

But it is not just the billionaires. Mid-tier Indian-Ugandan businesses run steel mills, sugar refineries, textile factories and pharmaceutical plants. Uganda Revenue Authority Commissioner General John Musinguzi has publicly praised the community's improving tax compliance, noting that the country's tax-to-GDP ratio has climbed to 14 percent — still below the 20 percent target needed for meaningful development, but trending upward in part because of Indian-owned enterprises formalising their operations.

Uganda's imports have shrunk by an estimated $500 million over four years, a decline Museveni himself attributes largely to Indian-owned local manufacturing displacing foreign goods.

## The Diaspora Angle

For the 1.8 million-strong Indian diaspora spread across dozens of countries, the Uganda story is both inspiring and cautionary. It demonstrates that a small, cohesive community can punch far above its weight economically — but it also raises uncomfortable questions about visibility, vulnerability and dependence.

In the United States, Indian Americans contribute an estimated five to six percent of all federal income tax despite comprising just 1.5 percent of the population. In Britain, Indian-origin entrepreneurs are responsible for a disproportionate share of small-business creation. The pattern repeats in the Gulf states, in Southeast Asia, in the Caribbean.

Yet the Ugandan experience is a reminder that economic success does not guarantee safety. The community was expelled once before, and while today's political climate is vastly different, the concentration of economic power in a minority group always carries risk.

## What Comes Next

Museveni, now in his fourth decade in power, clearly sees the Indian community as central to his industrialisation agenda. His government has rolled out investment incentives, including tax holidays and streamlined land-access programmes, to encourage further diaspora participation.

The question is whether this symbiotic relationship can survive a political transition. Uganda's economy is growing, but its youth unemployment rate remains stubbornly high, and populist sentiment against economically dominant minorities is never far from the surface in any country.

For now, the Indian-Ugandan community is doing what it has done for over a century: building, trading, and — as the tax rolls make clear — paying its share and then some. It is a remarkable story. Whether it remains a happy one depends on whether the next generation of Ugandan leaders is as pragmatic as the current one.

*The Indian diaspora in Uganda numbered approximately 40,000 as of 2025, according to Ugandan government estimates. President Museveni's remarks were made at a Diwali celebration attended by business leaders and diplomats.*
